provenance.platform: macOS 26.5.2 / arm64 / 12 cores / 24 GiB; file-backed flash emulation (FileFlash) plus one in-RAM SimFlash probe. NOT a Raspberry Pi, NOT an ESP32.
provenance.geometry: capacity 8388608 B, page 256 B, erase block 4096 B, data_base_offset 540672 , checkpoint slot 0 at 8192, slot 1 at 274432, THETA 16384, b_commit 8, durability OsCache
provenance.ground_truth: 48 distinct key/value records written and committed on every volume before the attack; each row reports how many still read back and how many returned a value differing from what was written
provenance.volumes: vol_single_epoch: engine epoch 2 after build, checkpoint write_offset 540672. vol_two_epochs: epoch 3, write_offset 3163648. vol_three_epochs: epoch 4, write_offset 5786624.

security_mode.note: FileCounter reports CounterKind::BestEffort, so the std path reports SecurityMode::BestEffortRollback — the honest G3 degradation: a counter file on a general-purpose filesystem can be snapshotted and restored together with the volume, so its monotonicity is only as strong as the surrounding system. A hardware monotonic counter (eFuse, RPMC-backed flash, or a TEE-held counter) declares CounterKind::Hardware and yields SecurityMode::Full, measured here via SimCounter. The boot rule executed is byte-identical in both modes: only the strength of the freshness tip differs. CounterKind::None would give NoRollbackProtection and skip the tip check entirely; no path in this run reported it.
security_mode.finding_genesis_mode_misreport: The mode reported immediately after a genesis format does NOT reflect the counter: `mount`'s FormatError branch constructs EngineState with a hardcoded BestEffortRollback, so a Hardware counter is reported as BestEffortRollback until the first remount, where it correctly becomes Full. This is a reporting defect only — a freshly formatted volume has no prior epoch to roll back to, so no rollback check is skipped — but any figure quoting security_mode must state whether it was read on genesis or on remount.

attacks.corrupted: 1 bit at flash offset 540700 (byte 0 of the ChaCha20-Poly1305 body of the first record on flash, which starts at 540672, total framed length 67, klen 11)
attacks.rationale: The record header is AEAD associated data and the body is the ciphertext, so a flipped body bit fails Poly1305 verification. `open_record` returns Error::Tampered and the replay scanner truncates the log at that record rather than applying it.

attacks.corrupted: 1 bit at flash offset 548886 (byte 0 of the ChaCha20-Poly1305 body of the last record on flash, which starts at 548858, total framed length 70, klen 11)
attacks.rationale: The record header is AEAD associated data and the body is the ciphertext, so a flipped body bit fails Poly1305 verification. `open_record` returns Error::Tampered and the replay scanner truncates the log at that record rather than applying it.

attacks.corrupted: 1 bit at flash offset 548859 (low byte of the `seq` field in the 28-byte record header at 548858; the header is the AEAD associated data)
attacks.rationale: The whole 28-byte header is passed as AEAD associated data, so mutating a header field that the codec still accepts (seq stays in range, magic and op untouched) is caught by the tag rather than by the parser.

attacks.corrupted: 1 bit at flash offset 548927 (last byte of the 16-byte Poly1305 tag of the record at 548858)
attacks.rationale: Forging the tag alone must also fail: verification compares the recomputed tag to the stored one, so corrupting the stored copy is indistinguishable from corrupting the body.

attacks.corrupted: flash offsets 548893..8388608 set to the erased byte 0xFF, cutting the record at 548858 (length 70) in half
attacks.rationale: A torn tail is the ordinary power-loss case: the truncated record has no valid commit marker above it, so the scan stops and the batch is never applied. This is the prefix-durability property the crash Monte-Carlo also exercises.

attacks.corrupted: 1 bit at flash offset 549381 (inside `seq_max` of commit-marker copy 1 at 549376; its 0x5C magic byte and copy 2 at 549632 are untouched)
attacks.rationale: This is the case the redundant marker pair exists for: copy 1 fails its HMAC-SHA256 check, the scanner falls through to copy 2, and the batch is applied normally.

attacks.corrupted: 256 bytes at flash offsets 549376..549632 zeroed (all of commit-marker copy 1, magic byte included); copy 2 at 549632 left valid
attacks.rationale: Zeroing the leading magic byte is not the same as corrupting the marker body: the scanner dispatches on the first byte at the offset, so it never reaches the verify-then-fall-back-to-copy-2 path and stops at that offset instead.

attacks.corrupted: 512 bytes at flash offsets 549376..549888 zeroed (both commit-marker copies of the last batch)
attacks.rationale: With no readable marker the batch it covers is unacknowledged by definition, so discarding it is the correct outcome, not a loss of durable data.

attacks.corrupted: 1 bit at flash offset 8268 (first sealed byte after the 76-byte header of checkpoint slot 0 at 8192, the newest checkpoint, epoch 2); slot 1 at 274432 left valid
attacks.rationale: Measures whether the two-slot checkpoint scheme can silently fall back to the older slot. It cannot: the older slot carries a lower epoch than the monotonic counter, so the O(1) freshness-tip check rejects it. Redundancy covers a crash inside the seal window, not deliberate corruption of the newest slot.

attacks.corrupted: 1 bit at flash offset 274508 (sealed body of checkpoint slot 1 at 274432, the superseded checkpoint); the newest slot 0 is untouched
attacks.rationale: Corrupting the superseded slot must be a no-op: `mount` picks the highest epoch among slots that pass their AEAD check, and that is still the newest slot.

attacks.corrupted: 1 bit in each checkpoint slot's sealed body (offsets 8268 and 274508); no slot passes its AEAD check
attacks.rationale: With no slot authenticating and at least one slot non-erased, `mount` must refuse rather than fall back to formatting a fresh volume — formatting would silently discard every durable record.

attacks.corrupted: whole data.bin replaced by an earlier, internally consistent image of the same volume (checkpoint epoch 1); counter.bin left at the current value (checkpoint epoch 2 was sealed against it)
attacks.rationale: Every byte of the replayed image is authentic, so no AEAD check can detect it. Only the monotonic counter can: the boot rule accepts a checkpoint epoch m only when m is the counter value or one above it, and a rolled-back image has m below it.

attacks.corrupted: data.bin from a later image of the same device (checkpoint epoch 3) paired with counter.bin from an earlier one (matching epoch 1)
attacks.rationale: The upper half of the boot rule. A gap of more than one epoch between the checkpoint and the counter cannot arise from a crash inside the seal window, so it indicates a spliced pair of authentic-but-mismatched artefacts and must be refused.

attacks.corrupted: 256-byte page of authentic sealed records copied from flash offset 540672 (below the checkpoint write offset 3163648, so sealed in an earlier epoch) over the page at 3163648 (in the replayed tail of the current epoch)
attacks.rationale: Splicing needs no key: the attacker relocates the engine's own authentic output. The record's AEAD tag still verifies, because the epoch travels in the authenticated nonce and its key is re-derivable. What fails is the batch's hash chain: the commit marker commits to a chain value over the records actually written there, so the batch does not match and is dropped.

attacks.corrupted: 1 bit in the HMAC-SHA256 tag of each of counter.bin's two 40-byte slots (offsets 8 and 48); the stored counter values are left intact
attacks.rationale: The software counter authenticates each slot with a key derived from the device key, so a value the attacker cannot re-MAC is unusable. With neither slot verifying, the freshness tip is unavailable and the mount must be refused rather than proceeding without a rollback check.
